entities.summary:
Physical geography is the branch of geography that studies Earth’s natural systems—landforms, climate, soils, water, biota, and their spatial patterns—often contrasted with human geography’s focus on societies. Although environmental description is ancient, modern physical geography took shape with Enlightenment and nineteenth-century earth science, notably through Alexander von Humboldt’s integrative measurements of climate, vegetation, and elevation.

The field absorbed geology, meteorology, hydrology, and ecology, developing quantitative and field methods to explain landscapes as dynamic process systems rather than static inventories. In universities it became one of geography’s two major pillars, informing resource management, hazard science, and later Earth-system and climate research.

Physical geography thus bridges natural science and spatial analysis, remaining essential to understanding environmental change, human–environment interaction, and planetary limits.
